script.text: A million-dollar math riddle, unsolved since eighteen fifty-nine. Did an AI just crack it?

The Riemann hypothesis predicts a hidden order in the prime numbers. On November twentieth, Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge said he found a proof with Claude, the company's AI. He posted a four-page note and a proof a computer can check.

That proof is written in Lean, where software checks every step. A day later, the teams behind Lean and its Mathlib library said the statement and proof check out, according to reports. MIT's Andrew Sutherland says he rechecked it independently.

But a machine check is not understanding. No human-readable proof is published yet, and number theorist Andrew Granville called the note garbled. The Clay Institute still lists the problem as unsolved. And Stanford posted a rival, all-human draft that same day.
Will mathematicians accept the AI-assisted proof within a year? Yes or no?

upload.title: AI-Assisted Riemann Proof Passes a Machine Check #shorts
upload.description:
On November 20, 2026, Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge said he had found a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, posed in 1859, working with the company's AI Claude, and released a four-page note plus a proof formalised in the Lean proof language. According to reports, the Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative said on November 21 that the formal statement and proof are correct, and MIT's Andrew Sutherland reports an independent recheck. The work is not peer-reviewed, a human-readable proof has not yet been published, number theorist Andrew Granville criticised the write-up, and the Clay Mathematics Institute still lists the problem as unsolved. On the same day, Stanford's Ravi Vakil posted a separate, human-written draft by Alessandro Masullo.

Sources: The Washington Post, Scientific American, Nature (news), Forbes, Phys.org, The Decoder, IBM Think, Washington Times, Clay Mathematics Institute (Millennium Prize Problems).
